cluster_name: Trump bars CNN, Politico, MS NOW; judge orders access restored
tldr: Across all ten country buckets, the dominant headline frame is judicial: court orders, judges blocking bans, and TRO compliance. Roughly half the headlines report the press-grounds ban reversed by a federal judge; the other half report CNN's exclusion from Air Force One, which received equal international billing but went unframed as a legally distinct action. Only Reason's headline explicitly questions whether the Air Force One exclusion is lawful, surfacing a distinction invisible in all other outlet titles. The Independent's 'Truth Social tantrum' and the New Yorker's 'The President vs. the Press' signal that UK and opinion-press headlines frame this as structural executive antagonism rather than a legal dispute.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only headline that frames the Air Force One exclusion as a separate legal question with a likely pro-executive answer ('Very Likely Yes'), while all other outlets treat the two bans as equivalent press-freedom violations.
Only headline using editorialised language ('tantrum'), departing sharply from the neutral descriptive framing used by every other outlet covering the same Air Force One exclusion.
Only title that embeds Trump's own 'fake news' characterisation of the banned outlets inside the headline itself, implicitly reproducing his framing while reporting the court order against him.

bottom_line: Headline coverage splits between a court-victory narrative—judge restores access—and an escalation narrative—CNN excluded from Air Force One—with only Reason's title signalling that the two incidents carry different legal weight. The LEGALITY frame dominates internationally; the POLITICAL frame, foregrounded in UK and opinion-magazine titles, treats the ban as an expression of executive temperament rather than a procedural legal dispute.
